claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 3F-J.

claims.claim: Kcnk16 L114P mutation leads to disruptions in both islet composition and secretion giving rise to a MODY-like phenotype in adult mice.
claims.source: Together, these results indicate that Kcnk16 L114P mutation leads to disruptions in both islet composition and secretion giving rise to a MODY-like phenotype in adult mice.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings.

claims.claim: Perforated patch-clamp recordings revealed blunting of β-cell Vm depolarization and loss of action potential firing in islets from Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice.
claims.source: Perforated patch-clamp recordings revealed blunting of β-cell Vm depolarization and loss of action potential firing in islets from Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Kcnk16 L114P β-cells showed blunted glucose-stimulated Vm depolarization, which did not reach a depolarized threshold to fire action potentials in 67% of β-cells.
claims.source: Similar to the whole islet recordings, Kcnk16 L114P β-cells showed blunted glucose-stimulated Vm depolarization, which did not reach a depolarized threshold to fire action potentials in 67% of β-cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by electrophysiology recordings from individual β-cells shown in the supplementary figure.

claims.claim: 33% of Kcnk16 L114P β-cells showed glucose-stimulated action potential firing, indicating that these cells may also undergo Ca2+ entry and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
claims.source: However, as 33% of Kcnk16 L114P β-cells showed glucose-stimulated action potential firing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), this indicates that these cells may also undergo Ca2+ entry and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that some β-cells retain electrical activity.

claims.claim: Reduced glucose-stimulated islet Vm depolarization and action potential firing in Kcnk16 L114P β-cells was in part a result of increased whole-cell two-pore domain K+ channel currents at depolarized Vm.
claims.source: Reduced glucose-stimulated islet Vm depolarization and action potential firing in Kcnk16 L114P β-cells was in part a result of increased whole-cell two-pore domain K+ channel currents at depolarized Vm and thus reducing K+ channel activity with high KCl depolarized these cells (Figure 4C and D; Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by whole-cell current recordings shown in Figure 4C and D and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: TALK-1 L114P (L/P and P/P) channels did not show a substantial increase at hyperpolarized β-cell membrane potentials under low and high glucose where these K+ currents are typically active.
claims.source: However, TALK-1 L114P (L/P and P/P) channels did not show a substantial increase at hyperpolarized β-cell membrane potentials under low and high glucose where these K+ currents are typically active (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by current-voltage relationship data shown in the supplementary figure.

claims.claim: Overexpression of the mouse mutant TALK-1 L114P channel results in large K+ currents indicative of a similar gain-of-function in mouse TALK-1 current as the human TALK-1 current due to the L114P mutation.
claims.source: Indeed, overexpression of the mouse mutant channel results in large K+ currents indicative of a similar gain-of-function in mouse TALK-1 current as the human TALK-1 current due to the L114P mutation (Figure 4E and F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by whole-cell current recordings from HEK293T cells shown in Figure 4E and F.

claims.claim: TALK-1 L114P blunted islet glucose-stimulated [Ca2+]c influx in mice on both B6 and B6;CD-1 genetic backgrounds compared to WT controls.
claims.source: TALK-1 L114P blunted islet glucose-stimulated [Ca2+]c influx in mice on both B6 and B6;CD-1 genetic backgrounds compared to WT controls (Figure 5A–F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5A-F and supplementary figure.

claims.claim: Islets from male Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice showed a larger reduction in normalized Ca2+ peak and normalized area under the curve responses compared to their controls than islets from female Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice compared to their controls.
claims.source: However, islets from male Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice showed a larger reduction in normalized Ca2+ peak and normalized area under the curve responses compared to their controls than islets from female Kcnk16 L114P (L/P) mice compared to their controls (Figure 5A–F).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by quantification of calcium responses shown in Figure 5A-F.

claims.claim: TALK-1 L114P channels did not affect the basal Ca2+ levels at 2 mM G.
claims.source: TALK-1 L114P channels did not affect the basal Ca2+ levels at 2 mM G; however, the activity of these channels resulted in increased initial glucose-stimulated drop in [Ca2+]c (termed phase 0 response) compared to controls (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5A and supplementary figure.

claims.claim: The activity of TALK-1 L114P channels resulted in increased initial glucose-stimulated drop in [Ca2+]c (termed phase 0 response) compared to controls.
claims.source: TALK-1 L114P channels did not affect the basal Ca2+ levels at 2 mM G; however, the activity of these channels resulted in increased initial glucose-stimulated drop in [Ca2+]c (termed phase 0 response) compared to controls (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data showing the phase 0 response.

claims.claim: The increased phase 0 response suggests a reduction in endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca2+ ([Ca2+]ER) storage in Kcnk16 L114P islets.
claims.source: This suggests a reduction in endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca2+ ([Ca2+]ER) storage in Kcnk16 L114P islets.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased phase 0 response.

claims.claim: Kcnk16 L114P islets showed a complete lack of glucose-stimulated [Ca2+]c oscillations monitored at 9 mM G.
claims.source: Furthermore, Kcnk16 L114P islets also showed a complete lack of glucose-stimulated [Ca2+]c oscillations monitored at 9 mM G (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging data shown in the supplementary figure.

claims.claim: Kcnk16 L114P islets do not exhibit [Ca2+]c entry in response to tolbutamide.
claims.source: TALK-1 L114P-mediated β-cell Vm hyperpolarization overrides the Vm depolarization caused by KATP closure by tolbutamide. Thus, Kcnk16 L114P islets do not exhibit [Ca2+]c entry in response to tolbutamide.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging with tolbutamide stimulation.

claims.claim: Islets from Kcnk16 L114P mice showed equivalent KCl-stimulated [Ca2+]c entry compared to control islets.
claims.source: Interestingly, islets from Kcnk16 L114P mice showed equivalent KCl-stimulated [Ca2+]c entry compared to control islets; this suggests that the loss of glucose-stimulated [Ca2+]c influx in the Kcnk16 L114P islets occurs due to enhanced K+ ion flux through gain-of-function in TALK-1 activity (Figure 5G and H).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging with KCl stimulation shown in Figure 5G and H.

claims.claim: The loss of glucose-stimulated [Ca2+]c influx in the Kcnk16 L114P islets occurs due to enhanced K+ ion flux through gain-of-function in TALK-1 activity.
claims.source: Interestingly, islets from Kcnk16 L114P mice showed equivalent KCl-stimulated [Ca2+]c entry compared to control islets; this suggests that the loss of glucose-stimulated [Ca2+]c influx in the Kcnk16 L114P islets occurs due to enhanced K+ ion flux through gain-of-function in TALK-1 activity (Figure 5G and H).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that KCl can rescue Ca2+ entry.

claims.claim: TALK-1 channels are functional on the ER membrane where they provide a K+ countercurrent for Ca2+ release from the ER lumen.
claims.source: Our previous studies showed that TALK-1 channels are functional on the ER membrane where they provide a K+ countercurrent for Ca2+ release from the ER lumen (Vierra et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claims.claim: IP3-induced [Ca2+]ER release was enhanced in islets from Kcnk16 L114P mice compared to controls.
claims.source: Indeed, IP3-induced [Ca2+]ER release was enhanced in islets from Kcnk16 L114P mice compared to controls suggesting gain-of-function TALK-1 channels are localized to the ER membrane where they facilitate increased Ca2+ release from the ER lumen (Figure 5I and J).

claims.claim: Gain-of-function TALK-1 channels are localized to the ER membrane where they facilitate increased Ca2+ release from the ER lumen.
claims.source: Indeed, IP3-induced [Ca2+]ER release was enhanced in islets from Kcnk16 L114P mice compared to controls suggesting gain-of-function TALK-1 channels are localized to the ER membrane where they facilitate increased Ca2+ release from the ER lumen (Figure 5I and J).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of enhanced IP3-induced Ca2+ release.

claims.claim: Kcnk16 L114P islets exhibit increased expression of genes which regulate Ca2+-independent potentiation of insulin secretion such as Adcy5, Creb5, Adcyap1, and Adcyap1r1.
claims.source: We observed increased expression of many genes which regulate Ca2+-independent potentiation of insulin secretion such as Adcy5, Creb5, Adcyap1, and Adcyap1r1; genes that may promote Ca2+-independent secretion from Kcnk16 L114P islets (Hodson et al., 2014; Jamen et al., 2002).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA sequencing data and supported by citations to previous functional studies.

claims.claim: Adcy5 has been shown to amplify glucose-stimulated cAMP production, which enhances glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
claims.source: For example, Adcy5 has been shown to amplify glucose-stimulated cAMP production, which enhances glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
claims.evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Adcy5 function.

claims.claim: Elevation of cAMP through activation of the GLP-1 receptor (with 200 nM liraglutide) only increased glucose-stimulated [Ca2+]c oscillation frequency in WT islets and did not impact the loss of glucose-stimulated [Ca2+]c entry in Kcnk16 L114P islet.

claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by calcium imaging with liraglutide treatment shown in the supplementary figure.

claims.claim: Kcnk16 L114P islets exhibit broad changes in ion channel activity genes (e.g. Cacna1g, Cacng8, Scn5a, Pkd1l1, Kcnk2, Gabrg1, and Fxyd3).
claims.source: For example, broad changes in ion channel activity genes (e.g. Cacna1g, Cacng8, Scn5a, Pkd1l1, Kcnk2, Gabrg1, and Fxyd3) may contribute to altered Ca2+ handling in Kcnk16 L114P islets.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by RNA sequencing data.

claims.claim: Reduced Ca2+ entry in Kcnk16 L114P islets results in decreased expression of genes previously shown to be elevated in chronically depolarized Abcc8−/− β-cells such as Serpina7, Asb11, Sall1, and Aldh1a3.
claims.source: Reduced Ca2+ entry in Kcnk16 L114P islets results in decreased expression of genes previously shown to be elevated in chronically depolarized Abcc8−/− β-cells such as Serpina7, Asb11, Sall1, and Aldh1a3 (Figure 6A; Stancill et al., 2017).

results.result: The KCNK16 L114P mutation is associated with MODY and causes a gain-of-function in TALK-1 K+ channel activity. This mutation co-segregates with MODY in two independent families (one four-generation Australian family and one Japanese family) and results in significantly increased TALK-1 K+ flux.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C19, C21, and C24 establish the genetic association between KCNK16 L114P and MODY through independent family studies and functional characterization. The genetic evidence from two unrelated families strengthens the association, and the gain-of-function phenotype provides a mechanistic basis for the disease.

results.result: Kcnk16 L114P mice exhibit genetic background-dependent neonatal lethality. Heterozygous mice show nearly complete lethality in the C57BL/6J background, while homozygous mice show lethality around postnatal day 4 in the mixed B6;CD-1 background. Heterozygous B6;CD-1 mice survive to adulthood.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C37, C38, C116, C117, and C118 are well-supported by chi-square analysis of genotype ratios at weaning (Figure 1B) and survival data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C). The genetic background dependency is clearly demonstrated with appropriate statistical analysis showing significant deviations from expected Mendelian ratios.

results.result: Neonatal Kcnk16 L114P mice exhibit severe hyperglycemia due to complete loss of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion. This results from a complete absence of glucose-stimulated Ca2+ entry in β-cells, caused by TALK-1 L114P-mediated membrane hyperpolarization that overrides KATP closure.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C40, C41, C43, C46, C48, and C114 are strongly supported by converging evidence from blood glucose measurements (Figure 1C), plasma insulin levels (Figure 1D), in vitro insulin secretion assays (Figure 1E-F), and calcium imaging (Figure 1K-N). The mechanistic explanation is supported by the observation that KCl can rescue Ca2+ entry, indicating the defect is at the level of membrane potential.

results.result: Insulin treatment (0.2 U/kg/day Glargine Lantus) extends the lifespan of homozygous Kcnk16 L114P neonates, demonstrating that lethality results from hyperglycemia due to inadequate insulin secretion.
results.evaluation: Claims C5 and C49 are supported by survival curve data (Figure 1O) showing extended lifespan with insulin treatment. This rescue experiment provides strong evidence that neonatal lethality is specifically due to insulin deficiency rather than other developmental defects.

results.result: Hyperglycemia in neonatal Kcnk16 L114P mice is transient, resolving by postnatal day 10 when blood glucose becomes equivalent to wildtype controls. This demonstrates that the Kcnk16 L114P mutation can cause transient neonatal diabetes.
results.evaluation: Claims C42 and C102 are supported by longitudinal blood glucose measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) showing hyperglycemia at P1 and P4 that normalizes by P10. This temporal pattern is consistent with transient neonatal diabetes and represents a novel phenotype associated with KCNK16 mutations.

results.result: Adult Kcnk16 L114P mice develop glucose intolerance starting at 7-11 weeks of age, with reduced glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and plasma insulin levels. This phenotype is maintained with age and results from enhanced β-cell membrane hyperpolarization and reduced glucose-stimulated Ca2+ entry.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C9, C50, C51, C52, C62, C65, and C105 are well-supported by glucose tolerance tests at multiple ages (Figure 2A-C, Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2), plasma insulin measurements (Figure 3A-B), and in vitro insulin secretion assays (Figure 3D). The mechanistic basis is established through electrophysiology and calcium imaging data.

results.result: Male Kcnk16 L114P mice exhibit fasting hyperglycemia, which is associated with elevated glucagon secretion under fasting and euglycemic conditions. This indicates a non-β-cell-specific islet defect involving α-cell dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Claims C53, C54, C66, C67, C140, and C186 are supported by fasting blood glucose measurements (Figure 2B) and in vitro glucagon secretion assays (Figure 3E) showing elevated glucagon under low glucose (2 mM) and euglycemic (7 mM) conditions. The inference that fasting hyperglycemia results from elevated glucagon is reasonable given the known role of glucagon in hepatic glucose production.

results.result: Kcnk16 L114P mice show altered islet composition with increased α-cell (glucagon-positive) area per islet and a modest reduction in β-cell (insulin-positive) area per islet. This change is observed in both neonatal and adult pancreata.
results.evaluation: Claims C68, C69, C45, C106, and C148 are supported by immunostaining and quantification data (Figure 1H-J for neonates, Figure 3F-J for adults). The statistical significance is demonstrated for the increase in α-cell area, while the reduction in β-cell area is described as modest, which is appropriately qualified.

results.result: Kcnk16 L114P β-cells show blunted glucose-stimulated membrane potential depolarization and loss of action potential firing in 67% of cells. This results from increased whole-cell two-pore domain K+ channel currents at depolarized membrane potentials.
results.evaluation: Claims C71, C72, and C74 are supported by perforated patch-clamp recordings from whole islets (Figure 4A-B) and individual β-cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), along with whole-cell current measurements (Figure 4C-D). The percentage of affected cells is quantified, and the mechanistic link to increased K+ currents is demonstrated.

results.result: Despite causing severe functional defects, endogenous TALK-1 L114P channels show only modest increases in K+ current at hyperpolarized membrane potentials where these channels are typically active. Current density was not significantly different at the resting membrane potentials of β-cells under low or high glucose.
results.evaluation: Claims C75, C157, and C160 are supported by current-voltage relationship data (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) showing no substantial increase at hyperpolarized potentials. This surprising finding is important as it contrasts with the large gain-of-function observed in heterologous expression systems and suggests the presence of endogenous regulators.

results.result: Overexpression of mouse TALK-1 L114P in HEK293T cells results in large K+ currents representing a substantial gain-of-function (7.96-fold at −30 mV and 6.13-fold at 0 mV compared to wildtype), similar to the human TALK-1 L114P mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C76 and C156 are supported by whole-cell current recordings from HEK293T cells (Figure 4E-F) showing dramatic increases in current amplitude. The fold-change values are quantified and demonstrate that the mouse mutation has similar biophysical properties to the human mutation when expressed heterologously.

results.result: TALK-1 L114P blunts glucose-stimulated Ca2+ influx in islets from both genetic backgrounds, with male mice showing larger reductions than females. Female Kcnk16 L114P mice show significantly greater glucose-stimulated Ca2+ influx than males, correlating with less severe glucose intolerance.
results.evaluation: Claims C77, C78, C131, and C134 are supported by calcium imaging data (Figure 5A-F) showing sex-specific differences in Ca2+ responses. The correlation between Ca2+ influx and glucose tolerance is demonstrated through multiple complementary measurements (GTTs in Figure 2, Ca2+ imaging in Figure 5), providing strong evidence for sexual dimorphism in the phenotype.

results.result: Kcnk16 L114P islets show complete loss of glucose-stimulated Ca2+ oscillations and no Ca2+ entry in response to tolbutamide, but exhibit normal KCl-stimulated Ca2+ entry. This indicates the defect is due to enhanced K+ flux through gain-of-function TALK-1 channels rather than defective Ca2+ channels.
results.evaluation: Claims C82, C83, C84, and C85 are supported by calcium imaging experiments (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C-D for oscillations, Figure 5G-H for KCl response). The ability of KCl to rescue Ca2+ entry provides strong evidence that the Ca2+ machinery is intact and the defect is specifically at the level of membrane potential control.

results.result: IP3-induced ER Ca2+ release is enhanced in Kcnk16 L114P islets compared to controls, suggesting gain-of-function TALK-1 channels are localized to the ER membrane where they facilitate increased Ca2+ release. This is associated with an increased phase 0 response suggesting reduced ER Ca2+ storage.
results.evaluation: Claims C87, C88, and C81 are supported by acetylcholine-stimulated Ca2+ release measurements (Figure 5I-J) and analysis of the phase 0 response (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1). The inference about ER localization is reasonable given previous work cited (C86) showing TALK-1 function on ER membranes, though direct localization of the mutant channel is not shown.

results.result: Kcnk16 L114P islets show increased expression of genes regulating Ca2+-independent potentiation of insulin secretion, including Adcy5 (2.13-fold), Creb5, Adcyap1, Adcyap1r1, Slit1, and Srgap3. These changes may promote Ca2+-independent insulin secretion to compensate for reduced Ca2+ entry.
results.evaluation: Claims C89, C172, C174, and C175 are supported by RNA sequencing data (Figure 6) with validation by qRT-PCR (Figure 6D). The fold-changes are quantified and the genes are appropriately linked to Ca2+-independent secretion pathways through citations. However, the functional significance of these changes is speculative and not directly tested.

results.result: GLP-1 receptor activation with liraglutide (200 nM) increases glucose-stimulated Ca2+ oscillation frequency in wildtype islets but does not rescue the loss of glucose-stimulated Ca2+ entry in Kcnk16 L114P islets.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 is supported by calcium imaging experiments with liraglutide treatment (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). This negative result is important as it demonstrates that cAMP elevation alone cannot overcome the membrane hyperpolarization caused by TALK-1 L114P, despite upregulation of cAMP-related genes.

results.result: Kcnk16 L114P islets show upregulation of stress-associated, fibrosis-related, and inflammatory signaling genes, including dedifferentiation markers (Sox4, Sox6, Sox9, Hk2, Vim, Cd36), extracellular matrix genes (Col1a1, Col1a2, Col3a1, Col14a1, Col6a1, Dcn), and inflammatory genes (Cxcl1, Ccl2, Ccl11, Ccl22, Tgfb2, Il33, Il6), likely due to prolonged hyperglycemia.
results.evaluation: Claims C95, C96, C97, and C98 are supported by RNA sequencing data (Figure 6A) with appropriate citations linking these genes to stress, fibrosis, and inflammation. The inference that these changes result from hyperglycemia is reasonable but not directly tested. The gene expression changes are consistent with glucotoxicity, though causality is not established.

results.result: The MODY-associated Kcnk16 L114P mutation disrupts glucose homeostasis in adult mice resembling a MODY phenotype and causes neonatal lethality by inhibiting islet insulin secretion during development. This confirms the association of TALK-1 L114P with MODY-like diabetes.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C11, C70, C101, and C153 represent the main conclusions of the study, which are well-supported by the comprehensive characterization of the mouse model including neonatal phenotypes, adult glucose intolerance, insulin secretion defects, and mechanistic studies of β-cell function. The mouse phenotype recapitulates key features of human MODY.

results.result: Transient neonatal diabetic patients with unknown genetic diagnosis should be screened for mutations in KCNK16.
results.evaluation: Claims C103 and C190 represent clinical recommendations based on the mouse model findings. While the mouse data showing transient neonatal diabetes is solid (C42, C102), this recommendation is speculative as no human neonatal diabetes cases with KCNK16 mutations have been reported. The claim is noted as speculation in the evidence type, and clinical validation would be required before this recommendation could be considered supported.

results.result: TALK-1 is an islet-restricted target for diabetes treatment, and these data strengthen the rationale for designing TALK-1 inhibitors as a therapeutic modality for KCNK16-associated MODY and possibly other forms of diabetes.
results.evaluation: Claims C12, C104, C108, and C191 represent therapeutic implications that are speculative. While the study demonstrates that TALK-1 gain-of-function causes diabetes and that KCNK16 is highly islet-restricted (C20), no inhibitor studies or proof-of-concept experiments are presented. The therapeutic potential is a reasonable inference but remains to be validated experimentally.

results.result: Female Kcnk16 L114P mice develop only moderate glucose intolerance compared to males in both genetic backgrounds. Females show greater body weight gain due to increased lean mass, which might reduce glucose intolerance compared to males.
results.evaluation: Claims C56, C57, and C58 are supported by glucose tolerance tests (Figure 2E-G) and body composition analysis (Figure 2H, Figure 2—figure supplement 3). However, claim C59 about lean mass reducing glucose intolerance is speculative and not directly tested. The correlation is observed but causality is not established, making this inference uncertain.

results.result: Insulin sensitivity is not altered in Kcnk16 L114P mice, indicating that the reduction in glucose tolerance is primarily due to an islet secretion defect rather than peripheral insulin resistance.
results.evaluation: Claims C63 and C64 are supported by insulin tolerance test data (Figure 3C) showing no difference between genotypes. This is an important control experiment that localizes the defect to the pancreatic islets rather than peripheral tissues, strengthening the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: The metabolic and functional defects in Kcnk16 L114P mice are not due to altered islet mass or growth defects, as body weight and pancreas weight are unchanged between genotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C39, C44, C55, and C183 are supported by body weight measurements (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, Figure 2D) and pancreas weight measurements (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1F). This is important negative data that rules out developmental or mass-related explanations for the phenotype.

results.result: The Kcnk16 L114P mutation did not affect plasma and liver triglyceride and cholesterol levels in mice, despite a previous association between the T2D-associated KCNK16 SNP (rs1535500) and increased cholesterol in humans.
results.evaluation: Claim C61 is supported by lipid measurements (Figure 2—figure supplement 3G-J) showing no differences. This negative result is important as it suggests the L114P mutation may have different effects than the A277E polymorphism, or that the human association may not translate to mice.

results.result: Kcnk16 L114P islets show decreased Sst (somatostatin) expression, likely due to reduced δ-cell secretion. Hyperglucagonemia in TALK-1 L114P islets is likely due to loss of inhibitory paracrine signaling, primarily mediated by reduced somatostatin secretion.
results.evaluation: Claims C144 and C145 are supported by RNA sequencing data (Figure 6) showing reduced Sst expression. Claims C143 and C142 represent reasonable inferences based on the known biology of islet paracrine signaling and the lack of TALK-1 expression in α-cells (C141). However, direct measurement of somatostatin secretion is not provided, making the mechanistic link somewhat indirect.

results.result: The discrepancy between large gain-of-function in heterologous expression and modest currents in primary β-cells points toward unidentified endogenous regulators of TALK-1 activity. The subtle increase in β-cell K+ conductance correlates with a modest MODY-like phenotype, which may explain why both MODY families carry the same L114P mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C161, C162, C163, and C165 represent important mechanistic insights supported by the comparison between HEK293T cell recordings (Figure 4E-F) and primary β-cell recordings (Figure 4C-D, Figure 4—figure supplement 2). The inference about endogenous regulators is speculative but reasonable. The correlation between modest current changes and modest phenotype is well-supported, though the speculation about why this specific mutation is found in MODY (C165) is not directly testable.

results.result: 33% of Kcnk16 L114P β-cells showed glucose-stimulated action potential firing, indicating that these cells may undergo Ca2+ entry and glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.
results.evaluation: Claim C73 is supported by electrophysiology data (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) showing heterogeneity in β-cell responses. This observation is important as it may explain why insulin secretion is not completely abolished in the mutant mice. The inference that these cells contribute to residual insulin secretion is reasonable but not directly proven.

results.result: Some of the TALK-1 L114P-mediated reduction in glucose-stimulated Ca2+ influx could be due to altered ER Ca2+ handling, as TALK-1 channels are functional on both plasma and ER membranes. TALK-1 L114P increases β-cell ER Ca2+ release in response to muscarinic stimulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C167, C168, and C169 are supported by the demonstration of enhanced IP3-induced Ca2+ release (Figure 5I-J) and citations to previous work showing TALK-1 function on ER membranes (C86). However, the relative contributions of plasma membrane versus ER membrane effects to the overall phenotype are not quantified, making claim C167 somewhat speculative.

results.result: The timeline and severity of MODY-like diabetes development in Kcnk16 L114P mice (glucose intolerance at ~8 weeks in B6 strain) is consistent with human MODY patients who were diagnosed at 11 and 15 years of age with abnormal oral glucose tolerance tests.
results.evaluation: Claims C115, C125, C126, and C127 are supported by glucose tolerance test data at multiple ages (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1-2) and comparison to clinical data from MODY patients. The mouse model recapitulates the adolescent onset of glucose intolerance seen in human MODY, strengthening the validity of the model.

results.result: Disease severity is more prominent in the inbred B6 strain compared to the mixed B6:CD-1 strain, likely due to genetic diversity. The Japanese KCNK16 MODY family showed greater insulin requirement than the Australian family, suggesting diversity in diabetes phenotypes occurs with KCNK16 mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C128, C129, and C130 are supported by comparison of phenotypes across genetic backgrounds in mice and clinical data from two independent MODY families. The inference about genetic diversity contributing to phenotypic variability is reasonable and consistent with observations in other genetic diseases, though specific genetic modifiers are not identified.

results.result: The TALK-1 L114P mutation in KCNK16 is associated with MODY diabetes and represents a gain-of-function mutation. This mutation was identified in a four-generation family and subsequently confirmed in a Japanese family, with functional characterization showing increased K+ flux.
results.evaluation: All reviewers explicitly affirm this central finding. Reviewer 1 states 'the data are convincing,' Reviewer 2 notes 'this is a very nice paper with mechanistic insight and clear clinical importance,' and Reviewer 3 describes the work as 'convincing and solid' with 'convincing evidence supporting a causal role of the L114P gain of function TALK-1 mutation.' The genetic and functional association is accepted without challenge.

results.result: Neonatal lethality in Kcnk16 L114P mice is dependent on genetic background and zygosity. Heterozygous mice show nearly complete lethality in the C57BL/6J background, while homozygous mice show lethality in the mixed B6;CD-1 background, demonstrating genetic background-dependent penetrance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings without challenge. Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'they have to perform a couple of breeding tricks to find a model that is lethal in adult which might complicate the conclusions' but does not dispute the data. Reviewer 3 notes 'the neonatal diabetes phenotype...uncovered by the study have important clinical implications,' indicating acceptance of the lethality findings.

results.result: Neonatal lethality results from severe hyperglycemia caused by loss of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and complete absence of glucose-stimulated Ca2+ entry in neonatal islets. Insulin treatment extends lifespan, confirming that lethality is due to inadequate insulin secretion.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this mechanistic finding. Reviewer 1 states the mutation 'causes a gain-of-function to increase K+ currents and inhibit glucose-stimulated insulin secretion,' and Reviewer 3 notes 'the mutation increases neonatal lethality, owing to hyperglycemia caused by a lack of glucose-stimulated Ca2+ influx and insulin secretion.' The insulin rescue experiment is accepted as demonstrating causality.

results.result: The L114P mutation increases whole-cell β-cell K+ currents, resulting in blunted glucose-stimulated membrane depolarization, loss of action potential firing in most β-cells (67%), and loss of glucose-induced Ca2+ oscillations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these electrophysiological findings. Reviewer 1 states 'the mutation...causes a gain-of-function to increase K+ currents,' and Reviewer 3 notes the study demonstrates 'blunted glucose-stimulated insulin secretion as well as increased glucagon secretion.' The electrophysiology data showing reduced depolarization and action potential firing is not questioned.

results.result: Adult Kcnk16 L114P mice develop glucose intolerance starting in adolescence (7-11 weeks), with reduced glucose-stimulated insulin secretion and plasma insulin levels. This phenotype is maintained with age and resembles MODY diabetes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly affirm this finding. Reviewer 2 states 'the phenotype of the heterozygote model used have a MODY-like phenotype,' and Reviewer 3 notes 'adult mutant mice showed glucose intolerance and fasting hyperglycemia, which is attributed to blunted glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.' The MODY-like phenotype is accepted as convincingly demonstrated.

results.result: Male Kcnk16 L114P mice exhibit fasting hyperglycemia, which is attributed to elevated glucagon secretion under fasting and euglycemic conditions. This indicates a non-β-cell-specific islet defect involving α-cell dysfunction.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding. Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'increased glucagon likely results from paracrine effects in the islets,' and Reviewer 3 notes 'blunted glucose-stimulated insulin secretion as well as increased glucagon secretion.' The mechanistic interpretation linking elevated glucagon to fasting hyperglycemia is accepted without challenge.

results.result: Adult Kcnk16 L114P islets show altered islet composition with increased α-cell (glucagon-positive) area/islet and a modest reduction in β-cell (insulin-positive) area/islet.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these morphological findings. Reviewer 3 notes 'the complexity of TALK-1 expression and hormone secretion in different endocrine cell types and how it impacts glucose homeostasis is elegantly illustrated in the L114P TALK-1 mouse model.' The islet composition changes are treated as supporting evidence for the functional defects.

results.result: Male Kcnk16 L114P mice exhibit more severe glucose intolerance than females, with males showing greater impairment in glucose-stimulated Ca2+ influx. This sexual dimorphism may relate to protective effects in females.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledge this finding. Reviewer 2 notes as a strength that 'data from both female and male mice are presented,' and Reviewer 3 states 'male mice were more affected than female mice' and describes this as having 'important clinical implications.' The sex differences are accepted as a significant finding.

results.result: TALK-1 L114P blunts glucose-stimulated Ca2+ influx in adult islets, with complete loss of Ca2+ oscillations and no response to tolbutamide. However, KCl-stimulated Ca2+ entry remains intact, indicating the defect is due to enhanced K+ flux through gain-of-function TALK-1 channels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these calcium imaging findings. Reviewer 3 notes 'islets from adult mutant mice were found to have reduced Ca2+ entry upon glucose stimulation' and describes the study as 'well-executed and rigorous.' The mechanistic interpretation that KCl can bypass the K+ channel defect is not challenged.

results.result: IP3-induced ER Ca2+ release is enhanced in Kcnk16 L114P islets, suggesting gain-of-function TALK-1 channels are localized to the ER membrane where they facilitate increased Ca2+ release from the ER lumen.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this finding. Reviewer 3 states 'islets from adult mutant mice were found to have...enhanced IP3-induced ER Ca2+ release, consistent with previous studies from the group showing a role of TALK-1 in ER Ca2+ homeostasis.' This dual localization finding is accepted as consistent with prior work.

results.result: RNA sequencing reveals altered gene expression in Kcnk16 L114P islets, including upregulation of Ca2+-independent insulin secretion pathway genes (Adcy5, Creb5, Adcyap1, Adcyap1r1), ion channel genes, stress markers, dedifferentiation markers, extracellular matrix genes, and inflammatory signaling genes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these transcriptomic findings. Reviewer 3 states 'comparison of bulk RNA sequencing results from WT and mutant islets revealed altered expression of genes involved in β-cell identify, function and signaling, which also contributes to the observed islet dysfunction.' The gene expression changes are treated as supporting evidence for the complex phenotype.

results.result: Despite dramatic gain-of-function when overexpressed, endogenous TALK-1 L114P channels in primary β-cells show only modest increases in K+ currents at physiological membrane potentials. This discrepancy suggests unidentified regulators of β-cell TALK-1 activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. Reviewer 3 notes 'the authors carefully and thoroughly addressed limitations of their study and discussed future directions,' implicitly accepting the discussion of this discrepancy. The observation that endogenous currents are more modest than overexpression studies is treated as an important mechanistic insight.

results.result: The Kcnk16 L114P mutation causes transient neonatal diabetes (hyperglycemia resolves by P10), suggesting that neonatal diabetes patients with unknown genetic diagnosis should be screened for KCNK16 mutations.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support this clinical implication. Reviewer 3 states 'the neonatal diabetes phenotype...uncovered by the study have important clinical implications' and notes the study has 'potential clinical utility.' The recommendation for genetic screening is accepted as a logical extension of the findings.

results.result: TALK-1 is proposed as an islet-restricted therapeutic target for diabetes treatment, with the data strengthening the rationale for designing TALK-1 inhibitors as a therapeutic modality.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this therapeutic implication. Reviewer 1 states 'the work will be valuable for understanding islet function,' and Reviewer 3 notes 'the importance of TALK-1 in β-cell and islet function demonstrated by this study will prompt future efforts targeting this important channel for diabetes treatment.' The therapeutic potential is accepted as a significant implication.

results.result: Insulin sensitivity is not altered in Kcnk16 L114P mice, indicating that glucose intolerance is primarily due to an islet secretion defect rather than peripheral insulin resistance.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding without challenge. The insulin tolerance test data demonstrating normal insulin sensitivity is treated as supporting evidence that the phenotype is islet-centric. No reviewer questions this interpretation.

results.result: Changes in glucose homeostasis are not due to altered β-cell mass, as pancreas weight and β-cell area are largely unchanged in Kcnk16 L114P mice.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept this finding. The preservation of β-cell mass despite functional defects is treated as supporting the conclusion that the phenotype results from functional impairment rather than β-cell loss. No reviewer challenges the morphometric data.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on genetic association between KCNK16 L114P and MODY (C2, C19, C21, C24). Both evaluations find the evidence convincing and well-supported by independent family studies and functional characterization.

Complete agreement on genetic background-dependent lethality and survival phenotypes (C3, C37, C38, C116, C117, C118). Both accept the chi-square analysis and survival data, though peer review notes breeding complexity.

Strong agreement on neonatal diabetes mechanism involving insulin secretion defects (C4, C40, C41, C43, C46). OpenEval includes additional claims (C48, C114) about calcium imaging and KCl rescue. Peer review also includes insulin rescue (C5, C11, C49) in this evaluation.

OpenEval focuses specifically on insulin rescue experiment (C5, C49) as separate finding, while peer review groups this with broader neonatal diabetes mechanism. Both find evidence convincing for insulin deficiency causing lethality.

Both address transient neonatal diabetes (C42, C102), but OpenEval evaluates as SUPPORTED while peer review extends to clinical screening recommendations (C103, C189, C190) also as SUPPORTED. OpenEval treats clinical recommendations separately as UNCERTAIN (R19).

Strong agreement on adult MODY-like phenotype with glucose intolerance and insulin secretion defects (C8, C9, C50, C51, C52, C62, C65). OpenEval includes additional mechanistic claims (C105), both find evidence well-supported.
Perfect agreement on elevated glucagon secretion and fasting hyperglycemia (C53, C54, C66, C67, C140, C186). Both accept the mechanistic interpretation linking glucagon to hepatic glucose production.

Strong agreement on islet composition changes with increased α-cell area and modest β-cell reduction (C68, C69, C106, C148). OpenEval includes neonatal data (C45), both treat morphometric findings as supporting functional defects.

Agreement on electrophysiological findings showing hyperpolarization and increased K+ currents (C71, C72, C74). Peer review groups with broader mechanism (C6, C7), both accept the gain-of-function phenotype.

Agreement on modest current increases in native β-cells versus heterologous expression (C75, C157, C160). Peer review includes additional mechanistic interpretation (C158, C161), both find this discrepancy important for understanding endogenous regulation.

OpenEval evaluates HEK293T overexpression data showing dramatic current increases (C76, C156) as separate finding. Peer review does not separately evaluate this but accepts it as part of broader electrophysiological characterization.

Agreement on sex-specific differences in calcium responses and glucose tolerance (C77, C78, C131, C134). Both find sexual dimorphism well-supported and clinically significant, though peer review emphasizes this as a study strength.

Strong agreement on calcium imaging findings including oscillations and KCl rescue (C82, C83, C84, C85). Both accept that KCl can bypass the membrane potential defect, demonstrating intact calcium machinery.

Agreement on enhanced IP3-induced ER calcium release (C87, C88). OpenEval includes inference about ER localization (C81, C86), peer review explicitly notes consistency with previous TALK-1 ER studies. Both find dual localization supported.

Agreement on RNA sequencing findings showing altered gene expression (C89, C172, C174, C175 in OpenEval; C89, C92, C93, C95-C98 in peer review). Both accept transcriptomic changes as supporting islet dysfunction, though note functional significance is speculative.
OpenEval separately evaluates liraglutide negative result (C91) as SUPPORTED. Peer review does not separately address this finding but accepts overall characterization of cAMP pathway changes.

Both address stress/fibrosis/inflammation gene expression changes (C95, C96, C97, C98). OpenEval notes inference about hyperglycemia causality is not directly tested; peer review accepts as contributing to islet dysfunction.

OpenEval groups main conclusions (C10, C11, C70, C101, C153) as SUPPORTED. Peer review addresses these claims across multiple evaluations, particularly R5 for MODY-like phenotype. Both find overall conclusions well-supported.

Divergence on clinical screening recommendations (C103, C190). OpenEval evaluates as UNCERTAIN due to lack of human neonatal cases; peer review evaluates as SUPPORTED with important clinical implications. Different thresholds for clinical translation.

Divergence on therapeutic implications (C12, C104, C108, C191). OpenEval evaluates as UNCERTAIN lacking proof-of-concept experiments; peer review evaluates as SUPPORTED, accepting therapeutic potential as logical extension. Different standards for speculative claims.

Both address sex differences and body composition (C56, C57, C58). OpenEval notes C59 about lean mass causality is speculative; peer review accepts sex differences broadly. Partial overlap with R12 on sexual dimorphism.
Perfect agreement on normal insulin sensitivity from insulin tolerance tests (C63, C64). Both treat this as important control localizing defect to pancreatic islets rather than peripheral tissues.
Agreement on preserved body weight and pancreas mass (C39, C44, C55, C183). Both accept this negative data as ruling out developmental or mass-related explanations for phenotype.
OpenEval separately evaluates lipid measurements showing no differences (C61) as SUPPORTED. Peer review does not separately address this finding but accepts overall metabolic characterization.
